Volume 13 · Chapter 09

Contracts and dynamic incentives

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c08

By the endDerive optimal contracts under hidden action and limited commitment.

Volume 13 · Chapter 9

Pay for an outcome, induce an action, keep a promise

A firm can observe a worker’s output without observing the care that produced it. A wage that makes care attractive can impose risk or leave a rent. Deferring compensation can spread consumption across dates, but it also creates an exit decision and a payment obligation. A successful contract must survive each of these choices at the date when it is made.

Capability. Formulate and solve hidden-action contracts with global incentive constraints, prove when a statistic contains all useful contracting information, and derive finite dynamic and restricted self-enforcing contracts. Six original cases separate limited worker liability, risk sharing, later participation and voluntary employer payment. Twelve solved exercises test proofs and changed assumptions.

Prerequisites. Consumer and producer duality supplies convex support arguments; Uncertainty and information supplies expected utility and finite conditioning. Dynamic and repeated games develops continuation incentives and discounted-tail arguments. Information economics and screening studies private information before a contract. Here effort is chosen privately after acceptance. A public output does not make that effort publicly observed.

1. Global incentives in utility space

Begin with a finite action set A and a finite, nonempty signal set Ω. Action a has cost c(a) in worker utility units and induces probabilities pa(s)>0, summing to one. Output Y(s) is in currency units. The risk-neutral principal offers deterministic wages w(s) in a common interval I and recommends a target a*. The worker observes the offer, accepts or rejects for reservation utility r, privately chooses an action, and then the signal is realized and the wage is paid. In this section the signal is verifiable: a court or stipulated enforcement mechanism implements the announced payment. Observable information known to the parties need not have that property; Section 8 changes enforcement explicitly.

The worker has continuous, strictly increasing, concave monetary utility u on I and expected utility Σspa(s)u(w(s))−c(a). A wage floor may represent limited liability or a bound on the worker’s available wealth. Nothing in the static model finances a payment exceeding the principal’s cash: enforceability and adequate financing are assumptions here, rather than consequences of positive expected profit. There are no private types, side bets or privately chosen savings in this initial model.

IR: Σ pa*(s)u(w(s)) ≥ r+c(a*).
Global IC: Σ [pa*(s)−pa(s)]u(w(s)) ≥ c(a*)−c(a), for every a∈A.
Principal profit at the target: Σ pa*(s)[Y(s)−w(s)].

IR means individual rationality at acceptance. IC compares the target with every feasible action, including a middle action that may be more attractive than either endpoint. Mixed action deviations cannot improve if all pure-action comparisons hold: their expected utility is a probability-weighted average of those pure values. We use weak implementation: at a tie the worker follows the recommendation, and at an acceptance or continuation tie the worker participates. This selection convention is part of the contract model. Strict implementation requires strict relevant inequalities and can replace an attained optimum by an unattained infimum.

For a fixed target the expected output is fixed. Set v(s)=u(w(s)) and h=u−1 on J=u(I). The least expected wage problem is

C(a*) = infv∈J|Ω| F(v),   F(v)=Σ pa*(s)h(v(s)),
subject to pa*·v≥r+c(a*),   (pa*−pa)·v≥c(a*)−c(a) for all a.

Convexity proof. The interval J is convex, and every displayed constraint is affine in v; hence the feasible set is convex. For v,z∈J and θ∈[0,1], concavity gives u(θh(v)+(1−θ)h(z))≥θv+(1−θ)z. Applying the increasing inverse gives h(θv+(1−θ)z)≤θh(v)+(1−θ)h(z). Thus h and F are convex. If u is strictly concave, h is strictly convex; positive target probabilities make F strictly convex in the entire payment vector. Whenever a minimizer exists, it is then unique. Concavity without strictness does not give that conclusion. A compact wage interval gives existence for a nonempty feasible set by continuity and compactness; an unbounded interval needs a separate argument. The examples below provide explicit attainable bounds.

A global certificate, not an assumed necessity theorem. Write the finite affine constraints, including any finite wage-utility bounds, as Ajv≥bj. Suppose v* is feasible and there is a supporting vector g for F at v*, meaning F(v)≥F(v*)+g·(v−v*) throughout J|Ω|. If g=ΣjλjAj, λj≥0, and λj(Ajv*−bj)=0, then every feasible v satisfies

F(v)−F(v*) ≥ Σ λj(Ajv−Ajv*) = Σ λj(Ajv−bj) ≥ 0.

This proves global optimality. For differentiable F, take g=∇F(v*); for a quadratic we can also display the exact nonnegative remainder. No constraint qualification is needed to verify this sufficient certificate. We have not claimed that such multipliers must exist at every optimum. In particular, wage floors can prevent a uniform wage reduction and leave IR slack. After solving each target problem, compare its output less C(a) with every other target and the principal’s no-contract value, normalized to zero. Optimizing wages for H is not yet choosing H.

The timing and action-versus-participation distinction build on the previously inspected Holmström lecture slides dated 2 February 2016. The finite convex proof, wage floors and numerical contracts here are original.

2. Wealth changes which effort the firm will buy

Worked case 1: a bounded loss and an efficiency wedge

For this case, the worker is risk neutral: u(w)=w. Success probabilities are pH=4/5 and pL=1/5; costs are cH=3 and cL=0; reservation utility is zero. Success yields Y≥0 and failure zero. Both wages must be at least −B, where B≥0 is the worker’s enforceable loss capacity. Negative wages are payments from the worker to the firm; assuming such a transfer is collectible is an explicit institutional condition. Let d=wS−wF.

H versus L: (3/5)d≥3, so d≥5.
H participation: wF+(4/5)d≥3.

Every H contract has expected wage at least 3 by IR and at least −B+(4/5)5=4−B by the floor and IC. The bound is attained by wF=max{−B,−1}, wS=wF+5. Hence CH(B)=max{3,4−B}. At B=0 the unique optimum is (wS,wF)=(5,0): the worker receives expected pay 4, incurs effort cost 3 and earns rent 1. At Y=15 the firm’s profit is 8. A constant zero wage implements L at cost zero and profit 3. H is chosen, but its positive worker rent is a cost to the firm rather than destroyed social output.

For 0≤B<1, attaining 4−B forces both wF=−B and d=5, so the wage vector is unique. At B≥1, the minimum 3 can be attained by every

5≤d≤5(3+B)/4,   wF=3−4d/5,   wS=3+d/5.

These are exactly all optimal H wages: cost 3 forces the stated mean, IC gives the lower spread, and the failure floor gives the upper spread; the success floor is then automatic. The interval collapses at B=1 but is nondegenerate for B>1. Binding IR therefore does not imply a unique wage schedule. With strict H selection, d>5 is necessary. At B=0 expected wage must exceed 4, although contracts (5+ε,0) approach that bound as ε↓0.

Because both parties are risk neutral in this case, currency transfers cancel in their combined expected payoff. Full-information H produces net (4/5)Y−3, versus (1/5)Y under L, so H is first best exactly when Y≥5, allowing ties. Under B=0 the firm buys H only when (4/5)Y−4≥Y/5, or Y≥20/3. More generally its threshold is Y≥(5/3)max{3,4−B}; compare with zero as well. At Y=6, first-best H and L net values are (9/5,6/5), while the firm’s constrained H profit is 4/5, below L’s 6/5. Restricting liability can change the chosen action even without risk aversion. There is no risk-sharing loss to compute in this risk-neutral example.

3. Risk sharing with an exact global certificate

Worked case 2: buy incentives in utility units, pay in currency

The primitives now deliberately change. Let pH=2/3, pL=1/3, cH=1/2, cL=0, reservation utility r=1, u(w)=√w and w≥0. Success yields 12 and failure zero. Effort cost 1/2 is a utility cost, not a currency payment. Write x=√wS, y=√wF. H requires

(2/3)x+(1/3)y≥3/2,   (1/3)(x−y)≥1/2,   x,y≥0.

The candidate (x,y)=(2,1/2) makes both constraints equalities, giving wages (4,1/4) and cost 11/4. It is not enough to solve those two equalities and assume that both should bind. With p=(2/3,1/3) and d=(1/3,−1/3), the cost F(v)=Σpsvs2 has gradient (8/3,1/3)=3p+2d at the candidate. For any feasible v, the exact expansion is

F(v)−11/4 = 3[p·v−3/2]+2[d·v−1/2]+Σps(vs−v*s)2 ≥ 0.

Each term is nonnegative. The final term vanishes only at v*, proving the unique global optimum with multipliers (3,2). The worker’s utilities under H and L both equal 1: weak selection matters even though the wage optimum is unique. For strict H implementation, take v=(2+ε,1/2); all constraints hold strictly for ε>0, the cost exceeds 11/4 and approaches it. The weak optimum is an infimum under strict effort selection, not a strict optimum.

If H were verifiable, IC would disappear. Jensen’s inequality gives EHw≥(EH√w)2≥(3/2)2=9/4, attained by the constant wage 9/4. Thus incentive-induced wage risk raises the least expected bill by 1/2. This compares two contracts that give the same worker utility; it does not add worker utility to firm currency profit. Constant wages of 1 implement L at cost 1. With output 12, H profit is 21/4, L profit is 3 and no contract gives zero, so H is selected.

For a changed success output Y≥0, hidden H beats L when Y/3≥11/4−1=7/4, hence Y≥21/4. Verifiable H beats L when Y/3≥9/4−1=5/4, hence Y≥15/4. At either threshold the relevant profits are positive, so no contract does not undo that comparison. These are target-selection thresholds within the respective information regimes; they are not currency-valued “total surplus” obtained by subtracting the worker’s utility cost from revenue.

4. Which measurements can be discarded?

Return to the finite static model with common wage interval I. A statistic T:Ω→𝒯 partitions signals into nonempty fibers. Call T sufficient for action if the conditional law q(s|t)=pa(s)/Pa(T=t), s∈T−1(t), is the same for every action a. Positivity of all pa(s) makes every denominator positive. This is sufficiency for the specified family of action laws, not a claim that T predicts revenue perfectly.

Likelihood-ratio equivalence. Fix any target a*. If T is sufficient, pa(s)=Pa(t)q(s|t), so pa(s)/pa*(s)=Pa(t)/Pa*(t), a function of t alone. Conversely, suppose each ratio equals ra(T(s)). Summing within a fiber gives Pa(t)=ra(t)Pa*(t). Dividing the state probability by this total cancels ra(t), giving the same conditional law as under a*. This proves both directions for every action, including any actions beyond H and L.

Utility conditioning theorem. For any feasible contract let v(s)=u(w(s)), m(t)=Σs:T(s)=tq(s|t)v(s), and set w̃(s)=h(m(T(s))). Because m is a convex combination of points in J, the common wage bounds are preserved. For every action,

Σ pa(s)u(w̃(s)) = ΣtPa(t)m(t) = Σ pa(s)u(w(s)).

Thus all action utilities, every IC comparison and IR are unchanged. Jensen’s inequality for convex h gives h(m(t))≤Σq(s|t)h(v(s)). Average with Pa*(t) to obtain Ea*w̃≤Ea*w. If u is strictly concave, h is strictly convex, and equality requires v to be constant within every fiber; positivity rules out ignoring a positive-probability variation. So a least-cost contract cannot contain ancillary wage variation within a sufficient fiber. Additional state-dependent payment restrictions could invalidate the replacement; the theorem assumes only the common interval and the displayed utility constraints.

Extra contractible information can always be ignored, so enlarging the available signal cannot raise the minimum cost when the old contracts remain available. Strict improvement is a separate question. For example, if L is implemented by the least-cost constant wage at its reservation utility, additional information about effort need not reduce that bill. The finite theorem above proves removal of irrelevant risk; it is not a blanket strict-informativeness theorem. Stole’s September 1999 notes, pages 4–12, distinguish global IC, sufficient information and the conditions needed for a first-order approach. Our conditioning proof uses the finite global constraints directly.

Worked case 3: a second performance measure with a strict value

Keep the worker, costs and output from case 2. Add a verifiable binary signal Z, independent of success conditional on effort, with P(g|H)=2/3 and P(g|L)=1/3. In order (Sg,Sb,Fg,Fb), the joint laws are pH=(4/9,2/9,2/9,1/9) and pL=(1/9,2/9,2/9,4/9). The likelihood ratios pL/pH are (1/4,1,1,4). The statistic counting favorable observations, T=(2,1,1,0), is sufficient: in the middle fiber both conditional state weights equal 1/2 under each action. Keeping only Y would discard informative variation.

The candidate utility vector is v*=(9/5,3/2,3/2,3/10), corresponding to wages (81/25,9/4,9/4,9/100). Direct substitution gives pH·v*=3/2 and (pH−pL)·v*=1/2. Its cost is 49/20. For d=pH−pL,

2pH(s)v*s=3pH(s)+(4/5)ds for each state.
F(v)−49/20 = 3[pH·v−3/2]+(4/5)[d·v−1/2]+ΣpH(s)(vs−v*s)2.

This globally certifies the unique optimum. Relative to output-only cost 11/4, the reduction is 3/10. In the sufficient middle fiber the utility payments coincide, exactly as the theorem predicts. If instead Z were conditionally distributed the same way under every action given Y, conditioning it out would preserve incentives and weakly lower cost. Its label or a correlation with output would not alone establish incentive value. Measurement cost, manipulability and whether the signal is actually contractible remain separate questions.

5. A stationary effort is not necessarily implementable

In a continuous-action model the agent’s first-order condition is necessary at a differentiable interior best response. Replacing global IC by that equation enlarges the candidate set. Solving the relaxed problem is useful only with a proof that the chosen action maximizes utility over the entire action domain. A correct derivative cannot repair the wrong feasible set.

Worked case 4: the first-order condition selects a minimum

Let e∈[0,1], success probability p(e)=1/4+e²/2 and effort cost c(e)=e/2. The worker is risk neutral and receives wF=0, wS=1. Probabilities stay between 1/4 and 3/4. Expected utility is

U(e)=1/4+e²/2−e/2 = 1/8+(e−1/2)²/2.

The derivative vanishes at e=1/2, but this is the unique minimum, worth 1/8. Both endpoints give 1/4. More strongly, no pair of finite binary wages implements any interior effort in this technology. For arbitrary spread Δ=wS−wF, utility is wF+Δ(1/4+e²/2)−e/2. If Δ>0 it is strictly convex and every interior value lies strictly below a convex combination of endpoint values. If Δ=0 it is strictly decreasing. If Δ<0 its derivative Δe−1/2 is negative everywhere. Thus a maximum is always at an endpoint. Changing the fixed wage cannot alter this conclusion.

Now change the technology to p(e)=1/4+e−e²/2, keeping wages and cost. Then

U(e)=1/4+e/2−e²/2 = 3/8−(e−1/2)²/2.

The same stationary effort is the unique global maximum, worth 3/8. This time the completed square proves implementation. In a general binary model, let Δu=u(wS)−u(wF)≥0. If p is concave, c is convex, and both are differentiable on an interval, then u(wF)+p(e)Δu−c(e) is concave. A zero derivative at an interior point is sufficient for a global maximum, since concavity bounds every other value by the tangent. Strict concavity gives uniqueness. Boundary optima use the corresponding one-sided inequality. These conditions establish effort optimality for the given contract; IR and the principal’s contract optimization still require their own checks.

6. A finite promised-utility recursion, proved in both directions

Consider T dates, finite action and signal sets at each date, positive action-conditional signal laws, and known calendar-specific primitives. Conditional on the current action, the next signal is drawn from its specified law independently of earlier actions and signals. There is no persistent hidden type or state. Wages belong to fixed compact intervals; u is continuous and increasing there, and costs and output are bounded because their sets are finite. The worker consumes each wage at receipt, cannot privately save or borrow, and has additive discounted utility; the principal is risk neutral with additive profit. Let worker discount β and principal discount δ lie in (0,1], which is harmless in a finite horizon.

The contract class consists of deterministic wage trees and pure recommended actions at every public signal history. There is no public lottery in this theorem. The worker may deviate using arbitrary behavioral actions depending on all its private and public history. The principal commits to the entire payment tree, including histories following a worker deviation. Optional worker exit is specified separately: at selected continuation dates the worker may leave irrevocably for a known continuation utility Rt, measured at that date. We solve contracts that retain the worker at every prescribed continuation, with continuation at equality. Exit values and other primitives may depend on the calendar, but not on an omitted payoff-relevant historical state.

Use t for the number of dates remaining, suppressing the associated calendar subscripts on primitives. Let Dt be the attainable expected-utility promises delivered by contracts in this class that are sequentially incentive compatible at every continuation. Let Vt(U) be the maximum principal continuation profit among such contracts delivering U exactly. At zero dates D0={0}, V0(0)=0, and all other promises are infeasible, written V0(U)=−∞. A required entry/exit bound is imposed by intersecting Dt with [Rt,∞) at the specified decision date; it is not silently imposed at every date.

The recursion chooses a current target a, wages ws and continuation promises Us. Whenever continuation exit is available, each Us must also satisfy its continuation reservation bound. With that restriction understood,

Vt(U)=max Σspa(s)[Y(s)−ws+δVt−1(Us)],
U = Σspa(s)[u(ws)+βUs]−c(a),
Σs[pa(s)−pa′(s)][u(ws)+βUs] ≥ c(a)−c(a′), for every a′,
ws in the wage interval;   Us∈Dt−1.

An empty feasible set means that U∉Dt and Vt(U)=−∞. Initial participation is handled by maximizing VT(U) over U∈DT with U≥r, then comparing with no contract. Replacing this inequality by U=r without proof would rule out contracts with unavoidable rents.

Step 1: continuation IC is sufficient against whole strategies. At the last date all-action IC compares every action directly. Inductively suppose each branch’s prescribed continuation is optimal for the worker after every possible private past. Private past actions have no effect on the branch’s future primitives or feasible actions, and there is no hidden wealth. Consequently, conditional on any realized next signal, a continuation deviation gives utility at most Us, including the option to exit. For any current action a′, its entire deviating continuation therefore gives at most Σpa′(s)[u(ws)+βUs]−c(a′). The current IC inequalities bound this by U. A mixed current action averages these bounds. This proves global continuation optimality at the current date and at every public history, including after privately deviating earlier.

Step 2: condition a feasible tree. Take any feasible t-date tree with current target a. Its continuation after s delivers some Us and satisfies the relevant participation bounds. A one-action deviation followed by its prescribed continuation proves the displayed current IC inequalities; conditional expectation proves promise equality. Its branch profit is no larger than Vt−1(Us). Thus its total profit is bounded above by the recursive objective at these controls. Taking the best tree gives the “no greater than” direction.

Step 3: stitch feasible continuations. Conversely, choose feasible controls and, after every signal s, a continuation tree attaining Vt−1(Us). Join them to the current wage/target node. Promise equality gives exactly U. Each continuation remains feasible; Step 1 makes the complete worker strategy optimal against arbitrary deviations. The resulting profit equals the recursive objective. Taking the best controls gives the reverse inequality. Replacing a continuation by a cheaper tree with the same promise changes neither the current incentive comparisons nor the utility of any current action. This is the precise reason the scalar promise suffices here.

Step 4: attainment is a finite-tree compactness fact. For a fixed finite pure recommendation tree there are finitely many wage coordinates, each in a compact interval. Every deterministic worker deviation is a map from a finite set of private/public histories to a finite action or allowed exit; there are finitely many such maps. Expected utilities under each map are continuous functions of the wage coordinates. At each continuation, weak IC, promise equality and any exit condition are therefore closed constraints. Mixed behavioral deviations add no restriction: backward optimization at finitely many histories selects a deterministic best response. The feasible wage set for that recommendation tree is closed in a compact product, hence compact. There are finitely many recommendation trees. Their finite union remains compact; its utility image is compact, and continuous principal profit attains a maximum on every nonempty fixed-promise slice. The same argument handles initial U≥r. Starting from t=0, this establishes the attained continuations used in Step 3, and an optimal full tree supplies maximizing recursive controls. No differentiability of V or convexity of D is needed.

The theorem does not establish optimality over additional randomized contracts. With persistent private types, hidden asset balances or history-dependent production, two workers with the same reported promise can face different future opportunities. One must then add a sufficient state and its incentive restrictions; the preceding induction cannot just forget the past. Principal commitment is also essential: Vt(U)≥0 at the beginning of a continuation does not prove that a particular discretionary payment will be made after output arrives. Section 8 tests that decision separately.

7. Deferral smooths consumption and creates a later participation test

Worked case 5: the contract must be reoptimized when the worker can leave

Use the case 2 probabilities, utility and costs. Hidden effort and output occur only at date 1; there is no date 2 production or effort. Both discount factors are 1. The firm commits to wages w1(s),w2(s)≥0; the worker consumes them when paid and cannot privately save or borrow. At entry the reservation utility for the entire relationship is 1. Initially there is no later exit option. All dates and rights are contractual, not claims about actual employment law.

Let xs=√w1(s), ys=√w2(s), zs=xs+ys. For fixed z≥0,

x²+y² = z²/2+(x−y)²/2 ≥ z²/2.

Equal utility at the two dates minimizes each branch’s wage bill: x=y=z/2. First-date IR and IC have exactly the case 2 form in z. The minimized cost is half its quadratic objective, so its same global certificate yields zS=2,zF=1/2. Wages at each date are (1,1/16), with expected total cost 11/8. Known H would permit constant branch utility 3/2, split 3/4 at each date, for cost 9/8. The hidden-action increment is 1/4. H profit is 8−11/8=53/8, exceeding L’s 4−1/2=7/2 and no contract. For L, the constant date wages (1/4,1/4) supply utility 1 without rewarding effort.

Now add a right to quit immediately before date 2 and receive an outside continuation utility b=3/4. Date 1 payments and effort are sunk then. The condition is ys≥b in each branch, not an unconditional initial inequality. The original failure continuation yF=1/4 fails this test, although original initial IR holds. Because the firm’s promise is enforceable only if the worker continues, quitting forfeits the remaining wage and replaces it by b. The new contract must retain the worker at every branch under the stated tie convention.

For a given total z, feasible splits require z≥b and y∈[b,z]. Completing the square around z/2 shows the global branch cost

gb(z) = z²/2 if z≥2b;
gb(z) = (z−b)²+b² if b≤z≤2b;
gb(z) = +∞ if z<b.

The optimal y is max{b,z/2} and x=z−y. The formulas coincide at z=2b. Their derivatives are 2(z−b) below 2b and z above it, agreeing at 2b and increasing throughout the domain. Thus gb is convex and increasing on [b,∞), strictly between distinct feasible points. H IC requires zS≥zF+3/2 and continuation participation requires zF≥3/4. Hence every feasible H contract has zF≥3/4 and zS≥9/4. Taking both lower bounds meets initial IR: expected gross utility is 7/4, so net utility is 5/4, above 1. Monotonicity of both branch costs now proves a unique global minimizing utility vector, without assuming initial IR binds.

At success the split is (x,y)=(9/8,9/8), giving wages (81/64,81/64); at failure it is (0,3/4), giving wages (0,9/16). The expected cost is 15/8. H remains selected: its profit is 49/8. For L, Jensen applied to convex gb and initial expected z≥1 gives cost at least gb(1)=5/8; the constant split (1/4,3/4) attains it and makes L strictly better than H. L profit is therefore 27/8. A wage cap of 4 would leave both H optima unchanged and put these cases within the compact domain of Section 6; the displayed lower-bound proofs also establish their optima without a cap.

The court’s ability to enforce a promise and the worker’s freedom to leave are different assumptions. Deferral can reduce the initial wage bill while making continuation participation more difficult. Stole, pages 36–40, discusses intertemporal contracting and credit-market restrictions. The finite recursion, constrained split and exit transfer above are proved independently; no asymptotic efficiency claim is used.

8. A bonus has to be attractive after the firm has received output

Now remove external enforcement of a success bonus. Specify the game rather than treating “trust” as an extra source of funds. Dates t=0,1,… have common discount 0<δ<1. In each period the worker privately chooses H or L; output S or F is drawn independently of the past conditional on that action and is publicly observed. The firm receives the output and then chooses an actual success payment x∈[0,b]; failure payment is fixed at zero. Payments are public. There is no persistent private state, private saving, legal recovery of an unpaid bonus, or separate salary choice. The number b≥0 defines the permitted payment range and the stationary promise class being examined; changing that class is a different model. Both parties are risk neutral, and the firm is assumed able to fund any allowed payment.

A public strategy uses the public output/payment history; the worker’s equilibrium strategy does not depend on unobserved past efforts. Call a profile self-enforcing in public strategies if, following every public history, it gives each party a best response against all feasible behavioral deviations, including the worker’s deviations based on its private past. Payment choices must also be optimal after each current output. This is a perfect-public-equilibrium style requirement for the specified game. We will prove it directly, because effort is hidden and the perfect-monitoring one-shot theorem from C07 does not apply without an additional argument.

Worked case 6: the exact interval of sustainable bonuses

Restore case 1’s risk-neutral production: pH=4/5, pL=1/5, cH=3, cL=0, success output 15 and failure output zero. There are two public states. In G, the worker chooses H and the firm pays b after success. A fully paid success or any failure leaves the state G. Any success payment x<b moves the relationship to B permanently. In B, the worker chooses L and the firm pays zero. In B the permitted success payments remain [0,b], but no payment restores G. Hidden effort itself never triggers a transition.

In B, L gives the worker 0 rather than −3; all positive payments reduce the firm’s current payoff and cannot improve future play. Thus B is credible at every history. Its expected per-period payoffs (firm,worker) are (3,0). At G, if the firm follows its strategy, future G is the same after either output; the worker’s complete current-action comparison is

(4/5)b−3 ≥ (1/5)b, or b≥5.

The expected cooperative payoffs are πG=12−4b/5 and uG=4b/5−3. At a success payment node, output 15 has already arrived. Paying b costs b now and preserves πG/(1−δ) from next period. Any x<b saves b−x now and replaces that continuation by 3/(1−δ). Among underpayments, x=0 is the most attractive. Therefore the necessary and sufficient payment comparison is

b ≤ [δ/(1−δ)](πG−3) = [δ/(1−δ)](9−4b/5).

Rearranging using 1−δ/5>0 gives 5≤b≤45δ/(5−δ). This interval is nonempty exactly when δ≥1/2. At equality only b=5 is allowed and H relies on weak effort selection. Strict effort incentives require δ>1/2 so that some b>5 is feasible; strict payment preference also requires b below the upper bound. These are necessity and sufficiency statements for the specified zero-salary success-bonus class and fallback, not a minimum patience theorem over all relational contracts.

For δ=3/5 and b=6, the upper bound is 135/22. The worker’s H-over-L gain is 3/5; expected worker and firm payoffs are (9/5,36/5). At a success, foregoing cooperation would sacrifice 63/10 of future firm profit, leaving payment margin 3/10. Joint expected payoff is 9 because both parties’ utility units here are the same currency units: transfers cancel, giving (4/5)15−3. The joint payoff under fallback is 3, so a punishment may invite mutually beneficial renegotiation even though neither party can improve by changing its own strategy alone.

Full deviation proof for the declared game. The inequalities above first verify one-period choices at both states. Fix the firm’s public strategy. At any worker decision, condition on its entire private history, including previous deviations. The current public state and chosen action determine the law of current output; its private past changes no current cost, probability or future opportunity. If it returns to the prescribed strategy after this choice, continuation values depend only on the public state. At G both outputs followed by prescribed payment retain G, so the H/L inequality is exhaustive. At B both outputs retain B and L is best. A randomized choice is an average of those two values. Thus the comparison is valid at every private history, rather than merely along the equilibrium path.

Fix instead the worker’s public strategy. At any firm payment node the current output is observed and its revenue is sunk. The continuation state is determined by the actual payment; the firm’s beliefs about past effort have no further payoff consequence. At G-success, the displayed inequality compares b with the best underpayment 0 and therefore with every x∈[0,b). At G-failure there is no payment choice. At B-success zero weakly dominates every payment in [0,b], and at B-failure there is no choice. These checks cover every public payment history, including histories following earlier underpayment.

To pass from these local checks to arbitrary deviations, first truncate a deviating strategy after K additional periods and require the prescribed strategy thereafter. Work backward through its finitely many time layers, first replacing the last altered payment choices, or the last worker action choices conditional on every private history, by prescribed choices. At the layer being replaced, all later choices already follow the profile, so the inequalities just proved apply pointwise; integrating over histories and randomization preserves the weak improvement. This is backward induction over time, not enumeration of payment histories: those histories may contain real-valued payments. Continue to the starting history. The truncated deviation cannot help. For fixed finite b, let M bound absolute stage payoffs for either party under all feasible moves. The difference between any deviation and its truncated version is at most 2MδK/(1−δ), uniformly over starting histories. Let K→∞. No arbitrary behavioral deviation improves, proving the stated public-strategy equilibrium claim. This proof uses the absence of persistent private state; public output alone would not supply it.

Levin’s May 2006 lecture notes, pages 1–2 and 5–6, motivate public relational strategies and separate discretionary-payment constraints. Our game restricts salaries and transfers, so its derived interval does not import the notes’ broader stationarity or surplus-division claims. The notes also distinguish unilateral enforcement from renegotiation and discuss why private monitoring needs additional analysis. Neither private monitoring nor general optimal relational contracting is proved here.

9. Exercises: prove feasibility before optimizing

Use exact fractions where possible. State the action recommendation and every applicable acceptance, exit and payment condition. Assume the chapter’s weak tie convention unless a prompt changes it. All numbers are synthetic; no observed empirical effect is supplied.

  1. Proof and timing. State the finite static contract timeline and distinguish observed from verifiable performance. Derive the utility-space feasible set, prove convexity of the inverse cost, and prove the multiplier certificate without asserting multiplier necessity. Explain precisely when uniqueness follows and why checking only a first-order condition for effort is insufficient.
  2. Wealth transfer. In case 1 derive CH(B) for every B≥0 and all optimal H wage vectors when B=2. Set Y=6 and find the smallest B at which H weakly beats L for the principal. Compare B=0 and B=1/2, first-best effort, no contract and strict effort selection.
  3. Risk and target selection. Starting from case 2’s laws, derive its wage vector and global certificate, the full-information H insurance bill and the hidden/verifiable H-versus-L output thresholds. Explain why uniqueness of wages does not imply strict effort implementation.
  4. A missed middle action. Add M to case 2, with pM=1/2 and cM=1/8. Keep the other actions, outside utility and wage floor. Does the old contract implement H? Find and globally certify the new least-cost H contract, checking H against both M and L. Report each action’s worker utility.
  5. Ancillary noise. Prove both directions of the likelihood-ratio sufficiency criterion and the utility-conditioning theorem for all actions. Then split each case 2 output into two equally probable ancillary labels under both actions. Give the success utility payments 2±1/4 and failure utility payments 1/2±1/4. Calculate the expected wage waste and construct its cost-reducing replacement.
  6. A measurement fee. Derive the four state probabilities and the optimal contract in case 3. Prove its global optimality. If installing Z costs the firm a nonrefundable fee k≥0 at contracting, while output-only wages remain available without the fee, find the fee at which the firm is indifferent between the two H contracts. Decide at k=1/4 and k=1/2. Explain whether using Z alone or grouping only the two middle states preserves the same information.
  7. FOA critique. Solve the worker’s global problem for the original case 4 wages and show that no binary wage pair implements any interior effort in the original technology. For the changed technology prove the unique interior optimum. State a sufficient concavity condition for a binary model and identify what it does not prove.
  8. Recursive proof and its boundary. State the full finite promised-utility recursion, terminal condition, current global IC and continuation participation restrictions. Prove the conditioning and stitching directions and explain compact attainment. Why do arbitrary private-history deviations add no profitable strategy under the hypotheses? Finally compare deterministic payment streams (1,0) and (1/4,1/4), both giving no-saving utility 1 with √w and β=1, when free zero-interest saving and borrowing are instead possible.
  9. Later exit. Derive the case 5 no-exit optimum and the branch cost gb. Reoptimize H for b=3/4, then compare H, L and no contract. Would b=1/4 change the original H contract? Explain why a court-enforced promise and worker continuation IR require different checks.
  10. Relational boundary. Derive the exact bonus interval in case 6, including both public states and all payment choices. For a fixed b=6 find the least discount factor permitting payment and effort under the weak convention. Is any H bonus in this class possible at δ=2/5? State what changes if H must be a strict best response.
  11. Punishing bad luck. Change case 6 so a failure also sends G to B; success with full payment retains G and any underpayment sends it to B. At δ=3/5,b=6 derive the firm’s and worker’s continuation values at G and B. Check current effort and payment separately. Can the original contract still be an equilibrium? Explain how the private-history/truncation proof would apply if all the changed local inequalities held.
  12. Research and institutional critique. A proposal says: “Every signal correlated with performance strictly reduces the optimal wage bill. A stationary effort equation proves implementation. Initial participation permits indefinite deferral. Positive expected continuation profit ensures voluntary bonuses will be paid, and δ≥1/2 is the universal relational-contract threshold.” Write a short corrective memo and a feasible evaluation design. Specify what data and institutional rights would be needed before estimating an effect of compensation on effort. Grade the argument by the explicit rubric in the solution rather than by whether it recommends adopting a bonus.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. The principal first commits to a wage schedule and target; the worker then accepts or rejects, chooses an unobserved action, and receives an enforced wage after a signal. Observation by the parties does not itself make the signal admissible to an enforcer. With v=u(w), all-action IC is (pa*−pa)·v≥c(a*)−c(a), and IR is pa*·v≥r+c(a*). These halfspaces intersect the convex interval product u(I)|Ω|. For v,z in u(I), concavity of u implies u(θh(v)+(1−θ)h(z))≥θv+(1−θ)z; increasing h reverses no inequality and yields convexity of h. Positive weighted sums preserve it.

    For a feasible v*, a supporting g=ΣλjAj with λ≥0 and complementary slackness gives F(v)−F(v*)≥Σλj(Ajv−bj)≥0. This checks global sufficiency and does not presume a constraint qualification. Strict concavity of u plus positive target probabilities makes the objective strictly convex, so two distinct minimizers would have a strictly cheaper midpoint, a contradiction. Existence still needs compactness or an explicit attained bound. A first-order action condition is merely local and can hold at a minimum, as case 4 proves; finite IC must include every action.

  2. IC gives d≥5; IR gives expected wage at least 3; the failure floor gives expected wage at least 4−B. The wages wF=max{−B,−1},wS=wF+5 attain both lower bounds as needed, so CH=max{3,4−B}. At B=2, every optimal vector is wF=3−4d/5,wS=3+d/5 for d∈[5,25/4]. The endpoints are (wS,wF)=(4,−1) and (17/4,−2); all intermediate values work. Their mean is 3 and their spreads satisfy IC.

    At Y=6, H beats L iff CH≤18/5. The smallest B is 2/5. At B=0 the profits (H,L,no contract) are (4/5,6/5,0); at B=1/2 they are (13/10,6/5,0). Thus the latter selects H strictly even though the selected wage leaves effort weakly tied. First-best H has combined net 9/5 versus 6/5, independently of the distribution of transfers. At the B=2 optimum any d>5 up to 25/4 strictly induces H at the same cost 3; at B=0 strict IC raises cost above its infimum 4. At B=2 worker participation remains a tie, which the stated convention resolves.

  3. Let v=(x,y). The mean and spread equalities give 2x+y=9/2 and x−y=3/2, hence v=(2,1/2). The cost is (2/3)4+(1/3)(1/4)=11/4. Its gradient (8/3,1/3) equals 3(2/3,1/3)+2(1/3,−1/3); the exact quadratic remainder in case 2 proves global optimality and uniqueness. Both H and L give utility 1, so uniqueness of the wage vector says nothing about strict action selection.

    Known H needs expected √w at least 3/2; Jensen makes constant wage 9/4 cheapest, a currency saving of 1/2 relative to hidden H. L’s constant wage 1 is cheapest by the same argument and strictly favors L. Comparing profits yields hidden threshold Y/3≥7/4, or Y≥21/4, and verifiable threshold Y/3≥5/4, or Y≥15/4. The associated profits exceed zero at the thresholds; for lower output compare the best remaining target with no contract. Strict H utility can be obtained by increasing x slightly, with cost approaching but never attaining 11/4.

  4. At the old contract, M gives (1/2)2+(1/2)(1/2)−1/8=9/8, exceeding H’s 1. Ignoring M invalidates implementation. The new H-versus-M condition is (1/6)(x−y)≥3/8, so x−y≥9/4, stronger than the L comparison x−y≥3/2. The candidate v*=(9/4,0) meets H IR at equality, meets H-versus-M at equality and respects the floor. Its wages are (81/16,0) and cost 27/8.

    For p=(2/3,1/3) and dM=(1/6,−1/6), its gradient (3,0)=3p+6dM. Therefore F(v)−27/8=3[p·v−3/2]+6[dM·v−3/8]+Σps(vs−v*s)²≥0 over the full feasible set; the H/L multiplier can be zero. Strict convexity makes the optimum unique. Utilities under (H,M,L) are (1,1,3/4). Weak recommendation selects H over M. The finite proof never assumes that the most distant action is the binding alternative.

  5. If pa(s)=Pa(t)q(s|t), every ratio pa/pa* depends only on t. Conversely, a fiber-constant ratio ra(t) also relates the fiber totals, so it cancels on conditioning. This proves equivalence. Replace v(s) by its conditional mean m(t) under the common q. Summing first within fibers and then over fibers preserves Eav for every a, so all IR/IC values are identical. Convexity of h makes h(m) no larger than the conditional mean of h(v), with a strict reduction when h is strictly convex and there is nonconstant within-fiber variation.

    The ancillary split has pH=(1/3,1/3,1/6,1/6) and pL=(1/6,1/6,1/3,1/3). The four utility payments are (9/4,7/4,3/4,1/4). Their within-output means remain (2,1/2), preserving both action utilities. The extra expected square is (2/3)(1/4)²+(1/3)(1/4)²=1/16; total cost is 45/16. Replacing the utility payments by (2,2,1/2,1/2), hence wages (4,4,1/4,1/4), reduces cost to 11/4. The added labels were irrelevant to every incentive comparison.

  6. Conditional independence gives the products (4/9,2/9,2/9,1/9) under H and the reversed endpoints under L. Substituting v*=(9/5,3/2,3/2,3/10) gives mean 3/2, utility difference 1/2 and cost 49/20. Its gradient equals 3pH+(4/5)(pH−pL); feasible slacks plus the positive quadratic remainder prove the unique global optimum. Thus the net H cost with measurement is 49/20+k versus 11/4 without it. The indifferent fee is 3/10. At k=1/4 the saving is 1/20; at k=1/2 measurement costs an extra 1/5. At output 12 both comparisons still favor the selected H contract over L or no contract.

    Z alone has the same binary laws as Y, so its minimum wage bill is only the output-only value 11/4; output revenue still follows Y, but its expectation for fixed effort is unchanged by which measure sets wages. Grouping Sb and Fg while retaining the two endpoints preserves the sufficient statistic T and cost 49/20. The argument assumes the fee changes neither laws nor worker preferences and that the additional measure is verifiable. It does not infer value from a sample correlation.

  7. For the original wages, U(e)=1/8+(e−1/2)²/2. The entire argmax is {0,1}, each worth 1/4; e=1/2 gives 1/8. For arbitrary binary wages, positive spread gives a strictly convex effort payoff, whose interior points are strictly below some endpoint. A zero spread leaves −e/2 plus a constant; a negative spread gives derivative Δe−1/2<0. Thus no interior effort is implementable by any finite pair, even if arbitrary negative wages were allowed.

    Under changed p(e)=1/4+e−e²/2, the payoff is 3/8−(e−1/2)²/2, giving a unique global maximizer 1/2. More generally Δu≥0, concave p and convex c imply concavity of u(wF)+pΔu−c. A zero derivative at an interior point then supports the whole function from above. Strict concavity implies uniqueness; no strictness is needed for weak optimality. This verifies the worker’s response for a stated wage schedule, not the principal’s global contract optimum or worker participation.

  8. With t dates remaining, maximize Σpa(s)[Y(s)−ws+δVt−1(Us)] subject to U=Σpa(s)[u(ws)+βUs]−c(a), all comparisons (pa−pa′)·[u(w)+βU]≥c(a)−c(a′), wage bounds and Us∈Dt−1. Impose Us≥Rt−1 only at specified continuation-exit dates. D0={0}, V0(0)=0, with other promises infeasible. Initial IR requires U≥r, not equality by definition.

    A feasible full tree induces these controls by conditional expectations; each branch’s profit is at most the best profit at its promise. Conversely, join feasible current controls to optimal branch trees. With no private state or credit, every private history faces the same future primitive problem once the public history is fixed. Induction makes branch continuations optimal against arbitrary deviations; averaging their bounds and applying current all-action IC proves optimality now. This proves both recursive inequalities. Compact wage boxes, finitely many recommendation trees and finitely many pure deviation maps give closed finite unions of compact feasible trees; continuous utility and profit then attain the required values. Randomized worker deviations add no gain by finite backward induction. This is not a theorem over additional public lotteries.

    Without private credit, both listed streams deliver utility 1. With unrestricted zero-interest intertemporal credit and nonnegative consumption, total resources W support maximum √c1+√c2=√(2W), attained at c1=c2=W/2. Thus (1,0) now gives √2, whereas (1/4,1/4) gives 1. Their equal no-saving promises no longer summarize their incentive value. Hidden wealth would add another omitted state. This establishes a failure of the stated scalar/no-saving calculation, not a proof that no recursive representation can ever handle saving.

  9. Given branch total utility z, x²+y²=z²/2+(x−y)²/2, so without exit x=y=z/2. The case 2 certificate in z gives (zS,zF)=(2,1/2); wages at each date are (1,1/16) and cost 11/8. With date 2 outside b, require y≥b, x≥0 and x+y=z. Minimizing the same square projects y=z/2 onto [b,z], yielding gb(z)=z²/2 for z≥2b, (z−b)²+b² for b≤z≤2b, and infeasibility below b.

    At b=3/4, H IC and the lower bound force zF≥3/4 and zS≥9/4. Those componentwise minima meet initial IR, and increasing g proves optimality. Success wages are (81/64,81/64); failure wages are (0,9/16). Cost is 15/8 and net worker utility is 5/4, so initial IR is slack. H profit is 49/8. For L, constant z=1 and split (x,y)=(1/4,3/4) attain cost 5/8; Jensen and IR prove no lower bill. Thus (H,L,no-contract) profits are (49/8,27/8,0), selecting H. At b=1/4 the original continuation utilities (1,1/4) satisfy the new bounds, so the unchanged original optimum remains globally optimal. Court commitment ensures payment conditional on continuation; it does not eliminate the worker’s contractual exit right.

  10. In B the worker strictly prefers L and the firm cannot restore G with a payment, so zero payment is optimal. In G future play under compliant payment does not depend on output, so H IC is (3/5)b≥3. At a success, the maximum one-shot saving is b from paying zero; the continuation loss is δ(9−4b/5)/(1−δ). Hence 5≤b≤45δ/(5−δ), feasible iff δ≥1/2. Failure creates no payment choice. Every intermediate underpayment saves less than zero payment but causes the same loss, so the comparison covers all x∈[0,b].

    For b=6, rearranging payment enforcement gives δ≥b/(9+b/5)=10/17; H is already strictly optimal because b>5. At δ=2/5 the upper bound is 90/23<5, so no H bonus exists in the specified class. If H must be strict, b>5 is required; the class needs δ>1/2, and no strict H contract exists at the endpoint. If payment must also be strict, use a bonus strictly below the upper bound. The chapter’s bounded-tail argument is needed to extend these local checks to arbitrary deviations.

  11. Use unnormalized discounted values. At B, firm value is 3/(1−δ)=15/2 and worker value is zero. At G, firm value P solves P=(4/5)(15−6)+δ[(4/5)P+(1/5)(15/2)]. Thus P=405/26, with P−15/2=105/13. Worker value W solves W=(4/5)6−3+δ(4/5)W, hence W=45/13. A current action changes both the success bonus and the chance of retaining G. H-over-L gain is (3/5)[6+δW]−3=24/13>0.

    After success, paying 6 preserves G while zero payment sends the firm to B. The future difference is δ(P−15/2)=63/13, less than 6; the payment margin is −15/13. The proposed profile fails: the firm wants to underpay even though worker effort has become more attractive. Punishing a failure shortens expected cooperation and changes both incentive problems. If all new local comparisons held, private past actions would still have no effect on future primitives; finite backward replacement and the uniform discounted-tail bound would establish global best responses exactly as in Section 8. One cannot retain the original continuation values after changing the transition rule.

  12. A defensible memo first writes the timeline and identifies the enforceable signal, available actions, utility units, wealth and credit restrictions, and who may exit or withhold payment. Correlation is not sufficient-statistic information for the action laws; ancillary wage variation wastes money in exercise 5, whereas exercise 6 proves a specific strict gain and prices the measurement fee. Replace the stationary equation by all-action or global effort comparisons: case 4 supplies a stationary minimum. Check each continuation IR separately: case 5’s original failure promise violates b=3/4, and its repaired optimum leaves initial IR slack. At each bonus-payment node compare the immediate saving with the actual continuation loss: exercise 11 fails that test despite positive continuation profits. Finally, δ≥1/2 characterizes one particular salary/bonus/fallback class; it is not a law of organizations.

    For evaluation, record contract versions, payment and exit dates, amounts actually paid, verifiability/dispute rules, outside opportunities, worker selection, measured outcomes and any credible independent effort or quality measure. A randomized, feasible change in the wage schedule among consenting eligible units, with predetermined outcomes, compliance tracking and spillover analysis, could identify an effect of that offered contract in that population. Without such assignment or another defensible identification design, high performers’ selection into bonuses and simultaneous technology changes confound a compensation/output correlation. Output is not effort itself; estimate a production/measurement model only with stated identifying evidence. Protect the distinction between a calibrated counterfactual and an observed causal result.

    20-point rubric. Award 2 for timing, units and rights; 4 for exhaustive IC and a valid global diagnostic; 3 for conditioning, strict-gain limits and measurement cost; 4 for saving restrictions and date-specific exit constraints; 4 for ex-post payment enforcement, fallback credibility and the restricted patience claim; 3 for a feasible identification/data plan with selection and measurement limitations. A recommendation either to adopt or reject the bonus can earn full credit. Ignoring a profitable deviation, treating unpaid promises as paid wages, or claiming causal evidence from the synthetic cases is a critical error requiring revision regardless of the total.

10. Teach-back, delayed recall and a research boundary

Teach-back. In five minutes explain why a large promised bonus can fail twice: it may leave an alternative worker action attractive, and it may be too tempting for the firm to withhold after success. Then explain why deferred pay requires a third test if the worker can leave.

Teach-back answer and retention answers

A complete explanation separates dates. Before effort, compare expected worker utility under every action, using the actual contingent wage or continuation utility. Before a later payment, compare continuing with the worker’s contemporaneous outside option. After output, when payment is voluntary, compare the firm’s current saving from withholding with the discounted loss of the specified continuation. Case 6 meets the first and third tests only inside its bonus interval; case 5 shows that initial participation alone does not meet the second. Do not describe output as observed effort, and do not treat a promise as its own enforcement mechanism.

  1. After two days: why use utility payments? They make every finite action comparison and IR affine, while the inverse utility makes the principal’s wage bill convex. The change of variables preserves the original constraints; replacing them by a stationary equation does not.
  2. After one week: when can a signal be removed? If conditional signal distributions within each statistic fiber are action independent, equivalently every action/target likelihood ratio is fiber-constant, averaging utility in the fiber preserves all action values and weakly lowers cost. Strict risk aversion makes genuine ancillary variation costly.
  3. After one week: is IR always tight? No. Case 1 at B=0 leaves rent 1; case 5 with later outside utility 3/4 leaves initial net utility 5/4 against reservation 1. Floors and continuation rights can block extracting the apparent slack.
  4. After one month: what makes one promise a state? History-independent future primitives, additive utility, no private wealth or persistent private type, and an enforced continuation tree. Condition and stitch at a fixed promise; then prove global worker IC. A scalar cannot simply erase omitted payoff-relevant information.
  5. After one month: why is positive continuation profit insufficient? An already received output does not reimburse a voluntary payment. The firm compares the payment with a difference of future values at that payment node. In exercise 11, positive G value still leaves a profitable underpayment.
  6. Transfer: does δ=1/2 solve every relational problem? It permits only b=5 with weak effort incentives in the stated zero-salary game. Different wages, outside values, private monitoring or transition rules need a new proof; the failure-trigger change already changes enforcement.

Reproducibility. Recreate the finite probability tables, check every action utility, and compute the quadratic certificates with exact fractions. Verify branchwise wage splits by the displayed square identity and voluntary payments by solving the two-state continuation equations. These are small exhaustive algebraic checks; a random grid cannot establish the global theorems. Editorial standard-library checks bind the working manuscript and verify its stated numerical anchors, while the proofs establish the continuum and infinite-horizon conclusions.

Source and extension scope. The reused Holmström record covers the earlier inspected static slides. Additional actual inspection for this chapter covers Stole’s stated static and two-date sections and Levin’s model/payment sections, with equation-page images retained in editorial provenance. Source hosting years are distinct from document dates. The general continuous first-order approach, optimal contracts with private savings, general infinite-horizon promise sets, renegotiation-proof implementation and private-monitoring relational contracts require further hypotheses and are not claimed proved here. The finite convex, conditioning, promise-recursion and restricted bonus theorems are fully proved above.

Next. Mechanism design and auctions turns from inducing a privately chosen action to designing allocation and payment rules for privately held information. The same discipline carries forward: identify the message or action space, compare every deviation, specify who pays whom and when, and separate a revelation argument from the stronger claim that a desired allocation is implementable.

Sources and further study

  • Bengt Holmström, MIT 14.124 Microeconomic Theory IV — Lecture Slides, Part 2 (Spring 2017 course; slides dated February 2, 2016) — Primary method reference for hidden effort and contractible outcomes, action and participation constraints, utility-space wage variables, informative performance measures and multitask attention allocation. The chapter's finite probabilities, limited-liability constraints, square-root risk example, audit and noisy-proxy technology are original and proved separately. C09 additional use: Prior static timing, utility-payment and incentive/participation context. Original chapter extends to explicit global proofs and wage bounds.
  • Lars A. Stole, Lectures on the Theory of Contracts, Sections 1–2, September 1999 revision — Finite/global action IC and verifiability; sufficient statistic factorization; limits of FOA and circular monotonicity argument; two-date utility-preserving wage variation, memory and credit-market restrictions.
  • Jonathan Levin, Relational Incentive Contracts, May 2006 lecture notes — Public-output hidden effort timing, public-strategy equilibrium definition, separate ex-post payment inequalities and renegotiation/private-monitoring caveats.
